```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = FALSE,
  comment = "",
  class.output = "spax-output",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  dpi = 100,
  # cairo writes smaller PNG files than the default macOS device (png only;
  # other devices, such as pkgdown's, get no extra arguments)
  dev.args = if (capabilities("cairo")) list(png = list(type = "cairo")) else list()
)
```

A floating catchment area (FCA) index measures access as supply per resident.
Each facility divides its supply, here GP full-time equivalents (FTE), by the
demand it can reach, here residents. Each place then adds up the ratios of the
facilities it can reach. Weights that fall with travel time decide what "can
reach" means, and the FCA methods differ in those weights. This guide computes
five indices on the same inputs, maps them on one color scale and shows how
much of the GP supply each one hands back to residents. By the end you can
choose an index and say what changes when you switch. The inputs are the
mainland grids of [The Cornwall GP example data](cornwall-data.html). The
`spax()` interface and the allocation model are experimental and may change
in later versions.

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
```

## The inputs

The setup code shared by every grid guide, explained in [The Cornwall GP
example data](cornwall-data.html), reads the population grid (residents per
grid cell), the mainland practices with their GP FTE excluding GPs in
training, and the travel stack: one raster layer of travel minutes per
practice. `prep_data()` holds them together for `spax()`.

```{r inputs}
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")[[gp$practice]]
# Keep cells with a travel time to every mainland practice
pop <- trim(mask(pop, sum(travel_grid)))
travel_grid <- crop(travel_grid, pop)
grid_data <- prep_data(pop, gp, travel_grid, id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
grid_data
```

```{r input-values, include = FALSE}
# Residents per cell as a plain vector, used by every comparison below
residents <- values(pop, mat = FALSE)
total_residents <- sum(residents, na.rm = TRUE)
supply_per_1000 <- 1000 * sum(gp$gp_fte_extg) / total_residents
```

The print gives the grid size, the `r nrow(gp)` practices and the supply
column. Its note means that a saved `grid_data` cannot be reused: run
`prep_data()` again after loading. The grid has
`r format(sum(!is.na(residents)), big.mark = ",")` populated cells holding
`r format(round(total_residents), big.mark = ",")` residents, and the
practices hold `r round(sum(gp$gp_fte_extg), 1)` GP FTE:
`r round(supply_per_1000, 2)` GP FTE per 1,000 residents across the mainland.

## Three ways to weight travel

The first three methods are the original two-step FCA (2SFCA), the enhanced
two-step FCA (E2SFCA) and the modified two-step FCA (M2SFCA). Each gathers
demand to practices with one set of weights, divides each practice's supply by
the demand it gathered, and spreads those ratios back to cells with a second
set of weights.

```{r gaussian-weights, include = FALSE}
kept <- round(100 * calc_decay(c(10, 20), method = "gaussian", sigma = 10))
```

Each method needs a rule for how much a practice counts at a given travel
time. A Gaussian decay is a bell-shaped weight: 1 at zero minutes, falling
smoothly as travel time grows. Its travel scale σ, in minutes, sets how fast
it falls: with σ = 10, a practice 10 minutes away keeps `r kept[1]`% of its
weight and one 20 minutes away `r kept[2]`%. The 15-minute catchment and
σ = 10 minutes are choices for this guide.

| Method | Weights when gathering demand | Weights when spreading ratios |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 2SFCA | 1 within 15 minutes, 0 beyond | The same |
| E2SFCA | Gaussian decay, travel scale 10 minutes | The same |
| M2SFCA | Gaussian decay, travel scale 10 minutes | The Gaussian weight squared |

You describe each index with a `spec_*()` function, which records the method
and its settings but no data. `spax()` then runs it on the prepared data.
`spec_2sfca()` takes the catchment as `threshold`. The other specifications
take a decay: `decay_gaussian()` here, or `decay_exponential()`,
`decay_power()`, `decay_step()` (a binary catchment) and `decay_inverse()`.

```{r methods}
gaussian_10 <- decay_gaussian(sigma = 10)

twosfca <- spax(grid_data, spec_2sfca(threshold = 15))
e2sfca <- spax(grid_data, spec_e2sfca(decay = gaussian_10))
m2sfca <- spax(grid_data, spec_m2sfca(decay = gaussian_10))

e2sfca
```

The print names the method, the grid, the `r nrow(gp)` practices and the
decay. The index itself is the raster `e2sfca$accessibility`, in GP FTE per
resident, so the maps multiply it by 1,000. Step 2 of [Inside the E2SFCA
calculation](e2sfca-steps.html) explains the print's last line, the demand
normalization.

The maps show the three surfaces in GP FTE per 1,000 residents on one color
scale.

```{r methods-map, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Three raster maps of mainland Cornwall on one color scale in GP FTE per 1,000 residents: E2SFCA changes smoothly, 2SFCA has sharp steps at the 15-minute catchment edges, and M2SFCA is lower throughout."}
# Stack the three surfaces and draw them on one shared color scale
all_three <- 1000 * c(
  e2sfca$accessibility,
  twosfca$accessibility,
  m2sfca$accessibility
)
names(all_three) <- c(
  "E2SFCA, Gaussian 10 min",
  "2SFCA, 15 min",
  "M2SFCA, Gaussian 10 min"
)
shared_range <- range(values(all_three), na.rm = TRUE)
# Mainland Cornwall's outline, in the grid's longitude and latitude
outline <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_union() |>
  st_transform(crs(pop)) |>
  vect()
plot(
  all_three,
  nc = 3,
  axes = FALSE,
  col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis"),
  range = shared_range,
  mar = c(1, 1, 2, 5),
  plg = list(title = "GP FTE\nper 1,000"),
  fun = function() lines(outline, lwd = 0.5)
)
```

E2SFCA changes smoothly. It is highest in the west, between Redruth, Truro
and Falmouth, and lowest on Bodmin Moor, the upland north-east of the map's
center. 2SFCA is patchy, with sharp edges where the 15-minute catchments end,
and its highest patches lie in the west and at the eastern edge near
Callington. M2SFCA has the E2SFCA pattern but is darker everywhere, for a
reason the next section shows.

## Compare the values

The table gives three cell quantiles and the index of the average resident,
for each method, in GP FTE per 1,000 residents.

```{r compare}
# Residents per cell, and each index per 1,000 residents, as plain vectors
residents <- values(pop, mat = FALSE)
per_1000 <- function(result) 1000 * values(result$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
e2sfca_values <- per_1000(e2sfca)
twosfca_values <- per_1000(twosfca)
m2sfca_values <- per_1000(m2sfca)

# Cell quantiles and the index of the average resident
describe <- function(index) {
  c(
    quantile(index, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE),
    resident_weighted = weighted.mean(index, residents, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}
round(
  rbind(
    E2SFCA = describe(e2sfca_values),
    `2SFCA` = describe(twosfca_values),
    M2SFCA = describe(m2sfca_values)
  ),
  2
)
```

```{r compare-values, include = FALSE}
weighted_m2sfca <- round(weighted.mean(m2sfca_values, residents, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
```

The quantiles describe grid cells, and most cells are rural. The
resident-weighted column answers a different question: what does the average
resident see? For E2SFCA and 2SFCA it equals the mainland ratio of
`r round(supply_per_1000, 2)` GP FTE per 1,000 residents. Each uses the same
weights in both steps and every practice gathers some demand, so the two
indices move supply between places without adding or losing any. M2SFCA gives
the average resident `r weighted_m2sfca`. Its squared weights are smaller
than the weights that gathered the demand, so part of the supply goes back to
no one, and cells whose practices are far away lose the most.

Correlations across cells show how far the surfaces agree on where access is
higher. The second output counts the residents with no practice within 15
minutes. 2SFCA gives them an index of zero.

```{r agreement}
# Correlation of E2SFCA with the other two, across cells
round(
  c(
    with_2sfca = cor(e2sfca_values, twosfca_values, use = "complete.obs"),
    with_m2sfca = cor(e2sfca_values, m2sfca_values, use = "complete.obs")
  ),
  2
)

# Residents with no practice within 15 minutes
round(sum(residents[twosfca_values == 0], na.rm = TRUE))
```

```{r agreement-values, include = FALSE}
two_digits <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
cor_2sfca <- two_digits(cor(e2sfca_values, twosfca_values, use = "complete.obs"))
cor_m2sfca <- two_digits(cor(e2sfca_values, m2sfca_values, use = "complete.obs"))
beyond_15 <- format(round(sum(residents[twosfca_values == 0], na.rm = TRUE)), big.mark = ",")
```

The three surfaces broadly agree: E2SFCA correlates at `r cor_2sfca` with
2SFCA and at `r cor_m2sfca` with M2SFCA. 2SFCA has sharp steps at the
15-minute edges, a longer upper tail and `r beyond_15` residents at zero. The
decay versions change gradually instead. The catchment and the travel scale are
choices, so it is
worth repeating a comparison like this one with the values you plan to use.
[Reading results](reading-results.html) says what an FCA index measures.

## Selection weights: 3SFCA and Huff-2SFCA

In the three methods above, the weights of all practices at one cell can add
up to more than 1: where many practices are close, each of them counts the
same residents. Two further methods, the three-step FCA (3SFCA) and
Huff-2SFCA, first share each cell's demand among the practices. At each cell,
the **selection weight** of a practice is its share of the cell's weights, as
the table defines, so the selection weights at a cell add up to 1. Both steps
then use the decay weight times the selection weight.

| Method | Selection weight of a practice at a cell | Weights in both steps |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 3SFCA | Its Gaussian weight, divided by the sum of these weights over the cell's practices | Decay weight × selection weight |
| Huff-2SFCA | Its Gaussian weight times its GP FTE, divided by the sum of these products over the cell's practices | Decay weight × selection weight |

Huff-2SFCA is named after the Huff model of where shoppers go, in which a
larger, nearer facility draws a larger share. Its selection weights multiply
each practice's decay weight by its attractiveness, by default its GP FTE
(`alpha = 1` is the power on GP FTE). To fit the Huff model itself to observed
registrations, see [Where do residents register?](allocation-workflow.html).

Both run like the others.

```{r selection-methods}
sfca3 <- spax(grid_data, spec_3sfca(decay = gaussian_10))
huff2sfca <- spax(grid_data, spec_huff2sfca(decay = gaussian_10))
```

```{r selection-range, include = FALSE}
# The next maps reuse the first map's color scale: check the new surfaces fit in it
selection_range <- 1000 * range(
  values(c(sfca3$accessibility, huff2sfca$accessibility)),
  na.rm = TRUE
)
stopifnot(
  selection_range[1] >= shared_range[1],
  selection_range[2] <= shared_range[2]
)
```

The maps put E2SFCA, 3SFCA and Huff-2SFCA on the color scale of the first
map, in GP FTE per 1,000 residents.

```{r selection-map, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Three raster maps of mainland Cornwall on the color scale of the first map, in GP FTE per 1,000 residents: E2SFCA changes smoothly and is low on Bodmin Moor and at the tips of the peninsulas, while 3SFCA and Huff-2SFCA are patchier, stay low on Bodmin Moor and are higher than E2SFCA at the tips of the peninsulas, most clearly at the Lizard."}
selection_maps <- 1000 * c(
  e2sfca$accessibility,
  sfca3$accessibility,
  huff2sfca$accessibility
)
names(selection_maps) <- c(
  "E2SFCA, Gaussian 10 min",
  "3SFCA, Gaussian 10 min",
  "Huff-2SFCA, Gaussian 10 min"
)
plot(
  selection_maps,
  nc = 3,
  axes = FALSE,
  col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis"),
  range = shared_range,
  mar = c(1, 1, 2, 5),
  plg = list(title = "GP FTE\nper 1,000"),
  fun = function() lines(outline, lwd = 0.5)
)
```

The same summaries as before compare the three.

```{r selection-compare}
sfca3_values <- per_1000(sfca3)
huff2sfca_values <- per_1000(huff2sfca)

# Cell quantiles and the resident-weighted index
round(
  rbind(
    E2SFCA = describe(e2sfca_values),
    `3SFCA` = describe(sfca3_values),
    `Huff-2SFCA` = describe(huff2sfca_values)
  ),
  2
)

# Correlations across cells
round(
  c(
    `E2SFCA, 3SFCA` = cor(e2sfca_values, sfca3_values, use = "complete.obs"),
    `E2SFCA, Huff-2SFCA` = cor(e2sfca_values, huff2sfca_values, use = "complete.obs"),
    `3SFCA, Huff-2SFCA` = cor(sfca3_values, huff2sfca_values, use = "complete.obs")
  ),
  2
)
```

```{r selection-values, include = FALSE}
cor_e2sfca_3sfca <- two_digits(cor(e2sfca_values, sfca3_values, use = "complete.obs"))
cor_3sfca_huff <- two_digits(cor(sfca3_values, huff2sfca_values, use = "complete.obs"))
```

The resident-weighted index is the same for the three. They differ in which
cells the supply is credited to. E2SFCA correlates at `r cor_e2sfca_3sfca`
with 3SFCA, while adding attractiveness to 3SFCA changes the surface less (a
correlation of `r cor_3sfca_huff`). On the maps, 3SFCA and Huff-2SFCA are
higher than E2SFCA at the southern tip (the Lizard) and the western tip
(Land's End), where E2SFCA is low. All three have their lowest values on
Bodmin Moor.

With `alpha = 0`, attractiveness has no effect and Huff-2SFCA gives the 3SFCA
surface:

```{r selection-alpha}
no_attractiveness <- spax(grid_data, spec_huff2sfca(decay = gaussian_10, alpha = 0))
all.equal(values(no_attractiveness$accessibility), values(sfca3$accessibility))
```

`selection` can give the selection weights another decay, for example
`decay_step(30)` to share each cell's demand only among practices within 30
minutes. `?spec_e2sfca` describes the options, and `?spax_3sfca` and
`?spax_huff2sfca` cite the methods.

## How much supply each index hands back

Multiply each cell's index by its residents and add up over cells: the result
is the GP FTE that the index hands back to residents. The table gives it as a
percentage of the total GP FTE.

```{r returned-supply}
# Residents times index, summed over cells, as a share of total GP FTE
returned <- function(result) {
  sum(residents * values(result$accessibility, mat = FALSE), na.rm = TRUE) /
    sum(gp$gp_fte_extg)
}
round(
  100 * c(
    E2SFCA = returned(e2sfca),
    `2SFCA` = returned(twosfca),
    M2SFCA = returned(m2sfca),
    `3SFCA` = returned(sfca3),
    `Huff-2SFCA` = returned(huff2sfca)
  ),
  1
)
```

```{r returned-values, include = FALSE}
returned_m2sfca <- round(100 * returned(m2sfca), 1)
```

This is the resident-weighted column of the tables above, divided by the
mainland ratio. The four indices that use the same weights in both steps hand
back all of the GP FTE, and M2SFCA hands back `r returned_m2sfca`%.

## Choosing an index

- **A fixed catchment**, such as a 15-minute standard: 2SFCA. Everyone beyond
  it gets an index of zero.
- **Access that fades with travel time**: E2SFCA, with a decay and a travel
  scale you choose. A Gaussian, exponential or power decay can also take a
  raster of σ values, for a travel scale that varies in space.
- **Remoteness counted against a place**: M2SFCA. It weights the ratios a
  second time on the way back, so a cell far from every practice gets a lower
  index even where those practices are not crowded. Part of the supply goes to
  no one, so its values are lower than those of E2SFCA.
- **Residents near many practices counted at most once**: 3SFCA, which shares
  each cell's demand among its practices. Huff-2SFCA also gives larger
  practices a larger share.
- **Expected use, fitted to where people register**: an allocation model,
  described in [An FCA index or an allocation model?](model-choice.html).

## A one-call shortcut

Once you have chosen an index, its one-call function computes it directly from
the inputs: `spax_2sfca()`, `spax_e2sfca()`, `spax_m2sfca()`, `spax_3sfca()`
or `spax_huff2sfca()`. The one-call functions take the travel stack as
`distance` and the decay as a list in `decay_params`. They return the same
object as `spax()`, so the E2SFCA surface is identical.

```{r one-call}
e2sfca_one_call <- spax_e2sfca(
  demand = pop,
  supply = gp,
  distance = travel_grid,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  id_col = "practice",  # matches supply rows to travel layers
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)
identical(values(e2sfca_one_call$accessibility), values(e2sfca$accessibility))
```

The one-call functions suit a single index. Specifications suit a comparison
like this one, where several indices run on the same prepared data.

## Several demand groups

Residents can differ in how far they travel, for example by age or by the
transport they have. Give `prep_data()` the demand as a named list of
single-layer rasters, one per group, and give the specification one decay per
group. Each group then gets its own surface.

The Cornwall data have no age split, so this section builds one. It assumes
that the share of residents in an older group rises in a straight line from
15% at the western edge of the grid to 35% at the eastern edge. It also
assumes that the older group travels less far to a practice, with a travel
scale of 8 minutes against 12 for the younger group. All of these numbers are
illustrative choices. The code builds the two group grids, prepares them, and
computes the index with one decay per group.

```{r groups}
# An illustrative older share that rises from west to east
older_share <- mask(init(pop, "x"), pop)
x_range <- unlist(global(older_share, range, na.rm = TRUE))
older_share <- 0.15 + 0.20 * (older_share - x_range[1]) / (x_range[2] - x_range[1])

groups <- list(
  younger = pop * (1 - older_share),
  older = pop * older_share
)
group_data <- prep_data(groups, gp, travel_grid, id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")

# One decay per group, named by the group IDs
by_group <- spax(
  group_data,
  spec_e2sfca(decay = list(
    younger = decay_gaussian(sigma = 12),
    older = decay_gaussian(sigma = 8)
  ))
)
names(by_group$accessibility)
```

All groups compete for the same GP time. The gathering step adds up the
demand of the groups that reaches each practice, each group with its own
weights, so a practice has one demand total and one supply-to-demand ratio.
The spreading step then gives each group its own surface from those shared
ratios, using its own
weights. The layer ending in `.all` is the overall surface: the average of the
group surfaces, weighted by each cell's demand. The maps show the three
layers on one color scale of their own, not the scale of the earlier maps.

```{r groups-map, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.4, fig.alt = "Three raster maps of mainland Cornwall on one color scale in GP FTE per 1,000 residents: the younger group, the older group with a shorter travel scale, which is lower everywhere, and the overall surface between the two."}
group_maps <- 1000 * by_group$accessibility
names(group_maps) <- c(
  "Younger, Gaussian 12 min",
  "Older, Gaussian 8 min",
  "Overall, demand-weighted"
)
plot(
  group_maps,
  nc = 3,
  axes = FALSE,
  col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis"),
  range = range(values(group_maps), na.rm = TRUE),
  mar = c(1, 1, 2, 5),
  plg = list(title = "GP FTE\nper 1,000"),
  fun = function() lines(outline, lwd = 0.5)
)
```

The older group's map is darker everywhere, and the overall map is close to
the younger one. The table gives the index of the average resident in each
group, and overall.

```{r groups-compare}
# Demand-weighted mean index per 1,000 residents of each group, and overall
mean_index <- function(layer, demand) {
  index <- 1000 * values(by_group$accessibility[[layer]], mat = FALSE)
  weighted.mean(index, values(demand, mat = FALSE), na.rm = TRUE)
}
round(
  c(
    younger = mean_index("gp_fte_extg.younger", groups$younger),
    older = mean_index("gp_fte_extg.older", groups$older),
    overall = mean_index("gp_fte_extg.all", pop)
  ),
  2
)
```

```{r groups-values, include = FALSE}
mean_young <- round(mean_index("gp_fte_extg.younger", groups$younger), 2)
mean_old <- round(mean_index("gp_fte_extg.older", groups$older), 2)
```

The average younger resident sees `r mean_young` GP FTE per 1,000 residents
and the average older resident `r mean_old`. The overall value lies between
them, nearer the younger group because that group is the larger one in every
cell. With a shorter travel scale, every practice at a positive travel time
gets a smaller weight for the older group, so its index is lower. The gap
comes from the assumed travel scales and the assumed split.

Transport modes work the same way. Split the residents by mode, for example
by the share of households with a car. Give `prep_data()` the demand as a
named list by mode, and the travel as a named list with the same names: one
travel stack per mode, naming the same practices in the same order. This
follows the multi-modal 2SFCA of [Tao et al.
(2018)](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-018-3132-8) (their equations 3-5), in
which the modes share the supply and the travel times differ by mode, and
extends it to a decay that differs by group. Earlier multi-modal 2SFCA work
includes [Mao and Nekorchuk
(2013)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.healthplace.2013.08.008) and [Langford,
Higgs and Fry (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.healthplace.2015.11.007). In a
specification, `decay` and `selection` can be a named list by group, and
`threshold` a named vector by group.
